clinicalPearls: Early, prominent and often refractory seizures are the hallmark, frequently out of proportion to other limbic features and sometimes progressing to status epilepticus.
It presents as a subacute limbic encephalitis with memory loss, confusion and behavioural change, usually in older adults.
There is a strong paraneoplastic association with small-cell lung carcinoma, so tumour screening is mandatory, particularly in smokers.
The receptor is a metabotropic (G-protein-coupled) inhibitory receptor, so antibody blockade removes inhibitory tone and drives hyperexcitability.
Co-existing antibodies may be present, and coexisting SOX1 antibodies further point to an underlying small-cell lung cancer.
Opsoclonus, cerebellar ataxia or brainstem features occasionally accompany the limbic syndrome.
Seizure control usually requires immunotherapy and, where present, treatment of the underlying tumour in addition to antiseizure drugs.
The combination of a smoker presenting with new severe seizures and amnesia should prompt urgent consideration of this diagnosis.
reference.pathophysiology: The GABA-B receptor is a metabotropic, G-protein-coupled receptor formed by GABA-B1 and GABA-B2 subunits that mediates slow, sustained inhibitory neurotransmission by opening potassium channels and inhibiting calcium channels and adenylate cyclase. It is densely expressed in the hippocampus, thalamus and cerebellum. Autoantibodies, predominantly of IgG1 subclass, target chiefly the GABA-B1 subunit and impair receptor function without necessarily destroying neurons, reducing inhibitory tone in limbic circuits. The resulting loss of GABAergic inhibition produces the intense epileptogenicity and hippocampal dysfunction that characterise the syndrome. The frequent link to small-cell lung carcinoma reflects a paraneoplastic mechanism in which tumour expression of neuronal antigens breaks immune tolerance; the concurrent presence of onconeural markers such as SOX1 supports this. Because IgG1 can fix complement, an element of inflammatory injury may contribute, and outcome is heavily influenced by whether an underlying malignancy is identified and treated.
additionalDifferentials: Anti-LGI1 and other antibody-mediated limbic encephalitides
Paraneoplastic encephalitis with classic onconeural antibodies (e.g. Hu)
New-onset refractory status epilepticus of other cause
Primary generalised or focal epilepsy of other aetiology
additionalInvestigations: Serum and cerebrospinal fluid cell-based assay for GABA-B receptor IgG
Urgent chest imaging and whole-body cross-sectional imaging to seek small-cell lung carcinoma
Testing for coexisting antibodies including SOX1 and other onconeural markers
Brain MRI for medial temporal signal change
Electroencephalography to characterise seizures and detect subclinical status
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis with oligoclonal bands and infection exclusion
Functional imaging where structural imaging is unrevealing and malignancy is suspected
redFlags: Refractory seizures or status epilepticus at presentation
New severe seizures and amnesia in an older smoker
Evidence of small-cell lung carcinoma on imaging
Rapidly progressive encephalopathy with reduced consciousness
Brainstem or cerebellar signs suggesting wider paraneoplastic involvement
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends heavily on detecting and treating any underlying small-cell lung carcinoma; with combined immunotherapy and oncological treatment neurological improvement is possible, but the presence of malignancy limits overall survival. Seizures often improve once immunotherapy is established.
pitfalls: Treating seizures with antiseizure drugs alone while missing the autoimmune and paraneoplastic basis
Failing to pursue repeated or thorough malignancy screening for small-cell lung carcinoma
Overlooking coexisting antibodies that signal an occult tumour
Attributing the presentation to a primary epilepsy syndrome in an older adult
Delaying immunotherapy while awaiting antibody confirmation in a compatible clinical picture
references: Autoimmune and paraneoplastic encephalitis consensus guidance
management: Urgent detection and treatment of underlying small cell lung carcinoma, the key determinant of outcome
First-line immunotherapy with corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange, escalating to rituximab or cyclophosphamide
Aggressive seizure control with combination antiseizure medication given the refractory epilepsy
Prompt management of status epilepticus in a high-dependency or intensive-care setting
Test for coexisting SOX1 antibodies that reinforce the search for small cell lung cancer
Ongoing tumour surveillance and multidisciplinary neurology, oncology and respiratory follow-up
